steps.premise: A whole loaf of each kind can be too much for one person to eat.
steps.action: Have bakers wrap some small portions of every loaf.
steps.consequence: Someone living alone can take home a variety they can use up.
steps.quote: Ask bakers to wrap a few small portions from each loaf so someone who lives alone can bring home several kinds without wasting bread.

steps.premise: A neighbor without an oven can still know an interesting bread.
steps.action: Accept contributions from a favorite local bakery.
steps.consequence: That neighbor can introduce the group to a loaf too.
steps.quote: Welcome a loaf from a favorite neighborhood bakery. Someone without an oven can make an introduction every bit as interesting as a home baker's.

steps.premise: A loaf's crust may give few clues to its filling or topping.
steps.action: Place ingredient cards beside the loaves with space to record those details.
steps.consequence: Visitors can find out what each bread contains.
steps.quote: Put blank ingredient cards beside the bread and leave room for fillings and toppings, which can be hard to identify from the crust.

steps.premise: Sharing cutting equipment can carry flavors from one loaf to another.
steps.action: Give each sample loaf a separate board and knife.
steps.consequence: A cinnamon slice keeps its own flavor after a visitor samples garlic bread.
steps.quote: Give each tasting loaf its own board and knife so the garlic on one sample doesn't follow the next visitor into a slice of cinnamon bread.

steps.premise: People coming from work may arrive after the first loaves go.
steps.action: With contributors' agreement, hold some bread for release later within the posted hours.
steps.consequence: Later arrivals can still pick from a selection.
steps.quote: Save some bread from willing contributors for a later release during the advertised hours, so arriving straight from work still means finding a choice.

steps.premise: Standing at the exchange can tire some visitors.
steps.action: Provide a stool at the exchange table.
steps.consequence: They can stay and talk with the bakers while seated.
steps.quote: A stool at the exchange table gives anyone who tires of standing a chance to linger and talk to the bakers.

steps.premise: Introducing oneself to a room can feel difficult.
steps.action: Invite bakers to leave a brief story with their loaf.
steps.consequence: Visitors have a specific detail they can ask about to start a conversation.
steps.quote: Invite people to put a few words about a loaf's history beside it. Asking about a grandmother's skillet bread is an easier opening than introducing yourself to a room.

steps.premise: Slices from different loaves may be hard to identify at home.
steps.action: Set out bags that hold several slices and a pencil to label them.
steps.consequence: People can tell which bread they brought home in each bag.
steps.quote: Set out paper bags big enough for a few slices and a pencil for writing on them, so people can tell their selections apart once they're home.

steps.premise: A contributor may need to leave briefly for an errand.
steps.action: Let a host look after the person's bread while they're out.
steps.consequence: They retain their place in the exchange.
steps.quote: Let contributors leave their bread with a host if they need to step out. A quick errand needn't cost them their place in the swap.

steps.premise: Rain can move the swap away from its usual courtyard.
steps.action: Include the indoor wet-weather location in the invitation.
steps.consequence: Neighbors carrying bread can go to the right place when it rains.
steps.quote: Post the indoor rain location with the invitation so a wet morning doesn't send neighbors carrying loaves to an empty courtyard.

steps.premise: A newcomer may need to see how an exchange works before the room fills.
steps.action: Put a volunteer at a quiet entrance welcome spot to walk them through a swap.
steps.consequence: They can learn the exchange process before it gets busy.
steps.quote: Place a quiet welcome at the entrance with a volunteer who can walk a newcomer through an exchange before the room gets busy.

steps.premise: People carrying trays need passing room, particularly near a display where people stop to ask questions.
steps.action: Space the displays far enough apart for two people with trays.
steps.consequence: Visitors can pass each other even where someone pauses.
steps.quote: Leave space between displays for two people to pass while carrying trays, especially where visitors tend to stop to ask about a loaf.

steps.premise: A visitor may hesitate to choose an unfamiliar loaf if unsure how to serve it the next day.
steps.action: Ask the baker how they like to eat it the day after, such as toasted or reheated.
steps.consequence: A serving suggestion makes the choice easier.
steps.quote: Ask each baker how they like to eat their bread the following day. A reheating or toasting suggestion makes a less familiar loaf easier to choose.

steps.premise: A conversation beside a display can tie up access to the bread.
steps.action: Place seats for talking a short distance from the table.
steps.consequence: People can keep chatting while others reach the loaves.
steps.quote: Put the conversation seats a little way from the bread so a good story can continue while somebody else reaches the table.

steps.premise: A visitor may want to bake a loaf they tried without exchanging contact details with a stranger.
steps.action: Provide slips for any willing baker to write out the recipe.
steps.consequence: Visitors can take the recipe and try baking it at home.
steps.quote: Offer recipe slips that bakers can fill in if they like, letting a visitor try the bread at home without asking a stranger for contact details.

steps.premise: A failed batch can leave a neighbor without a loaf to exchange.
steps.action: Reserve spare contributions in a basket for empty-handed guests.
steps.consequence: They can still come and take part.
steps.quote: Set a basket of spare contributions aside for people who turn up empty-handed. A batch that didn't rise shouldn't have to keep a neighbor away.

steps.premise: Newcomers may be unsure what amount makes a fair exchange.
steps.action: Display an actual example of the suggested portion near the entrance.
steps.consequence: Guests can judge a fair portion without guessing.
steps.quote: Show the suggested size of a swap portion with a real example near the door, saving newcomers the awkwardness of guessing what's fair.

steps.premise: Some people will miss out on a popular loaf.
steps.action: Offer its baker a place to leave a note about bringing it again.
steps.consequence: People who missed a share have a reason to come back.
steps.quote: Give the baker of a very popular loaf a place to leave a note about bringing it again, so missing out can turn into a reason to return.

steps.premise: Serving tins and baskets can be left for the hosts to deal with.
steps.action: State in the invitation when owners can pick them up.
steps.consequence: Owners know when to retrieve their things, reducing unclaimed kitchenware.
steps.quote: Keep the invitation clear about when people can collect their serving tins and baskets, sparing the hosts a pile of unclaimed kitchenware.

steps.premise: A child may want a role at the swap.
steps.action: Invite the child to draw a picture of a loaf for the display.
steps.consequence: The family has a way to help together while leaving the samples untouched.
steps.quote: A child who wants to help could draw a little portrait of a loaf for the table, giving families something to do together without handling the samples.

steps.premise: Steam trapped around a newly baked loaf can soften its crust.
steps.action: Provide a cooling rack near check-in for warm arrivals.
steps.consequence: A loaf can cool before bagging and keep its crust for tasting.
steps.quote: Leave a cooling rack near check-in for bread that arrives warm, since bagging a steaming loaf can soften the crust before anyone tries it.

steps.premise: The closing crew may have bread left over that belongs to contributors.
steps.action: Ask bakers ahead of time to choose where their spare bread should go.
steps.consequence: The crew can pass it along to a destination the baker agreed to.
steps.quote: Invite contributors to choose a home for their spare bread in advance, allowing the closing crew to pass it along with the baker's agreement.

steps.premise: A newcomer approaching from the street may already be managing a bike and a loaf.
steps.action: Put a sign at the entrance where people on the pavement can see it.
steps.consequence: First-time visitors can spot the way in as they approach.
steps.quote: Put a street-facing sign at the actual entrance. First-time visitors juggling a loaf and a bike will appreciate spotting the way in from the pavement.

steps.premise: Visitors may remember a bread they would enjoy tasting again.
steps.action: Give them a sheet to write down those requests.
steps.consequence: A neighbor familiar with a requested bread gets an idea for what to bring next time.
steps.quote: Keep a sheet where visitors can request a bread they remember fondly, giving a neighbor who knows how to bake it an idea for the next gathering.
